title: Fourths, fifths and the tritone
summary: The open, steady sound of 4ths and 5ths, and the restless tritone between them.

steps.title: Perfect 4th and perfect 5th
steps.body:
Five half steps make a **perfect 4th** (C to F). Seven make a **perfect 5th** (C to G).

They are called perfect because they sound so open and steady. The 5th is the sound of a power chord, and of the C and G you may already play in your left hand.

steps.title: The tritone
steps.body: Six half steps, right between the 4th and the 5th, is the **tritone** (C to F♯). It sounds tense, as if it wants to move somewhere. You will hear it inside the 7th chords that pull a song back home.

steps.title: 4th, tritone and 5th above C
steps.body: F is a perfect 4th above C, F♯ is a tritone, and G is a perfect 5th.

items.prompt: Play C4, then go up a perfect 4th.
Play C4, then go up a perfect 5th.
Play D4, then go up a perfect 5th.
Play G4, then go down a perfect 5th.
Play C4, then go up a tritone.

steps.title: Settled or restless
steps.body: Play a 5th with your left hand and move it around the keyboard. Then try a tritone. Notice how the 5th sounds settled and the tritone sounds restless.

items.prompt: Play E4, then go up a perfect 5th.
Play A4, then go up a perfect 4th.
